title: Was, were, and once upon a time
seoTitle: Was and were in Turkish: idi, imiş and -mış
intro: This unit puts **to be** in the past: *Dün evdeydim* (I was at home yesterday), *Hava soğuktu* (It was cold), *Burada bir fırın vardı* (There was a bakery here). It then shows a second past, `-(y)mIş`, for what you heard or found out rather than saw, and takes a first look at `-mIş` on verbs, the voice of every folk tale: *Bir varmış, bir yokmuş…* (Once there was, once there wasn't…).

blocks.text: To say **was** or **were**, add `-(y)DI` and a type II ending, the set you met with the [past tense](gp-past-di), to a noun, an adjective or a place word: *öğrenci* → *öğrenciydim* (I was a student), *evde* → *evdeydik* (we were at home). Turkish grammars call it the witnessed past of the copula (*ek fiilin görülen geçmiş zamanı*).

blocks.label: Past of to be
lines: after a vowel:  buffer y      hasta → hastaydı
f s t k ç ş h p: t            soğuk → soğuktu

blocks.text: After a vowel, the buffer y of [A1 unit 3](gp-buffer-letters) comes in: *hastaydım*, *evdeydin*. After a consonant there is no buffer, and the D follows the usual rule: *yorgundum*, *güzeldi*, but *soğuktu*, *Türk'tüm*. The I is in four-way harmony with the last vowel of the word.

rows.en: he or she was a student

blocks.text: For **they**, *öğrencilerdi* (plural first, then the past) is just as correct, and with a plural subject the bare *öğrenciydi* is common: *Çocuklar bahçedeydi* (The children were in the garden).

**Var and yok.** *Vardı* is **there was, there were**, and *yoktu* **there wasn't, there weren't**. With a possessive, as in [A1 unit 9](gp-possessive-have), they mean **had** and **didn't have**: *Arabam vardı* (I had a car), *Vaktim yoktu* (I didn't have time).
**Negative.** *Değil* takes the past and the ending, written as one word: *değildim* (I wasn't). Its l is voiced, so the D is always d.

**Questions.** The particle `mI` comes right after the word, and the past and the ending join it, all in one word: *hasta mıydın?* (were you ill?), *evde miydi?* (was she at home?). The particle follows the harmony of the word before it; the past ending follows the particle.

items.en: There used to be a bakery here.

items.tr: Dün yorgun değildim, ama bugün yorgunum.
items.seg: Dün yorgun değil|di|m, ama bugün yorgun|um.
items.en: I wasn't tired yesterday, but I am today.

blocks.text: In a question, `mI` comes **before** the past ending: *evde miydin?*, not *evdeydin mi?* This is the opposite of the past tense of verbs (*geldin mi?*), so watch the difference between a verb and **to be**.

blocks.title: Açtım: hungry or open?
blocks.text: *Açtım* is either **I was hungry** (*aç* + *-tım*) or **I opened** (*aç-* + *-tım*). Context always tells them apart.

sections.title: Hastaydı, hastaymış: two pasts of to be

blocks.text: Turkish has a second form, `-(y)mIş`, that marks what you didn't witness yourself: something you heard, read, or worked out. Compare *Ali dün hastaydı* (Ali was ill yesterday: I know, I saw him) with *Ali dün hastaymış* (Ali was ill yesterday, I hear). Turkish grammars call it the learned past of the copula (*ek fiilin öğrenilen geçmiş zamanı*).

It takes the buffer y after a vowel, never changes its m, and has four-way harmony. Its personal endings are type I, the endings of the present (see [the two sets](gp-person-endings-types)): *hastaymışım*, not *hastaymışm*.
Unlike `-(y)DI`, `-(y)mIş` doesn't fix the time. *Ali hastaymış* can mean **Ali was ill, I hear** or **Ali is ill, I hear**; context decides.

rows.en: he or she is ill, I hear

Example
Meaning
rows: Murat isn't (wasn't) at home, I'm told.
Apparently there used to be a bakery here.
It seems there are no free rooms at the hotel.
Was the exam hard, did they say?

blocks.text: **Discovery.** `-(y)mIş` also marks something you find out at this very moment, often with surprise: tasting the soup, *Bu çorba çok güzelmiş!* (This soup is really good!); reading a price tag, *Çok pahalıymış!* (It's so expensive!). *Meğer* (it turns out that) often comes with it: *Meğer bugün tatilmiş* (It turns out today is a holiday).

items.en: The exam was very easy, they say.
Ayşe wasn't at home yesterday, apparently.
This café is really nice! (you've just walked in)
It turns out Can was at home.

blocks.text: **İdi and imiş.** In formal and older writing, both forms can be written as separate words, *idi* and *imiş*, which never change their vowel: *hasta idi* = *hastaydı*, *öğrenci imiş* = *öğrenciymiş*, *var idi* = *vardı*, with endings *idim, idin…* You'll meet them in official texts, newspapers and older literature; in everyday writing use the suffixes.

English has no grammar for this. It uses words: **apparently**, **I hear**, **they say**, **it turns out**, **so…!** French does the same with paraît-il, or with the conditional of the news (il serait malade). Turkish builds it into the word.
Don't use `-(y)mIş` for what you saw yourself. If you watched the film and it was bad, say *Film kötüydü*; *Film kötüymüş* means someone told you so.

sections.title: Gelmiş: a first look at -mIş with verbs

blocks.text: Verbs take `-mIş` too, on the stem, with four-way harmony: *gel-* → *gelmiş*, *yap-* → *yapmış*, *oku-* → *okumuş*, *gör-* → *görmüş*. It starts with a consonant, so the stem never changes: *gitmiş*, *yemiş*, *demiş*. Turkish grammars call it the learned past (*öğrenilen geçmiş zaman*).
Where `-DI` reports what you saw or simply state as fact, `-mIş` reports what reached you some other way. It has three everyday uses:

items: **Hearsay**, what someone told you: *Elif İstanbul'a gitmiş* (Elif has gone to Istanbul, I hear).
**Inference**, from what you can see now: *Yağmur yağmış* (It has rained: the street is wet).
**Surprise**, a discovery: *Aa, kar yağmış!* (Oh, it's snowed!), on opening the curtains.

blocks.text: `-mIş` is also the tense of folk tales, jokes and legends, which nobody alive witnessed: *Bir varmış, bir yokmuş* (Once there was, once there wasn't), *Keloğlan bir gün şehre gitmiş* (One day Keloğlan went to the city). A [Nasreddin Hoca](a1-u04-culture) story is told the same way: *Hoca bir gün pazara gitmiş…*

rows.en: he or she has come, it seems

blocks.text: With *ben*, `-mIş` means you realize something only afterwards: *Uyumuşum* (I must have dozed off). The negative (*gelmemiş*), the question (*gelmiş mi?*) and the full range of uses come in [B1](gp-evidential-mis). For now, learn to recognize the form, and use it in the third person.

items.en: Ali's here! (you see his shoes at the door)
Elif has gone to Istanbul, I hear.

blocks.text: When you tell a joke or a story you heard, keep `-mIş` all the way through. Switching to `-DI` would mean you were there.

`-mIş` has four-way harmony: *gelmiş*, *almış*, *okumuş*, *görmüş*. Don't confuse it with the plain `-DI`: *gitti* (he went) and *gitmiş* (he has gone, I hear) are both correct, but say different things about how you know.

summary: **Was** and **were**: `-(y)DI` + type II ending on a noun, adjective or place: *öğrenciydim*, *yorgundu*, *soğuktu*, *evdeydik*.
*Vardı* and *yoktu*: there was, there wasn't; with a possessive, had: *Arabam vardı*.
Negative *değildim*; question *hasta mıydın?*, with `mI` before the past ending.
`-(y)mIş` marks what you heard, inferred or just discovered: *Ali hastaymış*, *Bu çorba çok güzelmiş!* It takes type I endings and doesn't fix the time.
In formal writing the separate words *idi* and *imiş* replace the suffixes: *hasta idi* = *hastaydı*.
On verbs, `-mIş` gives hearsay, inference and surprise: *Elif gitmiş*, *Kar yağmış!* `-DI` is for what you saw.
Folk tales and jokes are told in `-mIş`: *Bir varmış, bir yokmuş.*
